outcomes.text: Describe how eukaryotic cells differ from bacterial cells, including where the genetic material is held.
Use scale, size of cells and standard form for order-of-magnitude calculations.
Use the prefixes centi, milli, micro and nano.
Explain how the nucleus, membrane, mitochondria, chloroplasts and plasmids relate to their jobs.
List the parts of animal cells and the extra parts found in plant cells.
Estimate and compare the relative size of sub-cellular structures.
Use a light microscope to observe, draw and label plant and animal cells with a magnification scale.
Explain how the structure of specialised cells suits their function in a tissue, organ or organism.
Explain why cell differentiation matters and how plant and animal cells differ in when they differentiate.
Describe how microscopes developed and how electron microscopes revealed more cell detail.
Calculate magnification, real size and image size, giving standard form where suitable.
Describe chromosomes as DNA carrying many genes, found in pairs in body cells.
Describe the three stages of the cell cycle including mitosis and what each does.
Explain why mitosis matters for growth and recognise it in given contexts.
Describe stem cells and their role in embryos, adult bone marrow and plant meristems.
Evaluate benefits, risks and ethical issues of stem cell treatments and therapeutic cloning.
Explain how plant meristem cells let growers clone rare or crop plants quickly.
Describe diffusion and give examples of substances that move in and out of cells this way.
Explain how concentration gradient, temperature and surface area change the rate of diffusion.
Calculate and compare surface area to volume ratios.
Explain why large organisms need exchange surfaces and transport systems.
Explain how the small intestine, lungs, gills, roots and leaves are adapted for exchange.
State what makes an exchange surface effective: area, thin membrane, blood supply, ventilation.
Describe osmosis as water diffusing through a partially permeable membrane.
Calculate rate of water uptake and percentage change in mass of plant tissue, and plot graphs.
Investigate how salt or sugar solution concentration affects the mass of plant tissue.
Describe active transport against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration, with root hair and gut examples.
Compare diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
Order cells, tissues, organs and organ systems and explain how each builds on the last.
Understand size and scale from cells to tissues, organs and systems.
Describe enzymes as catalysts whose active-site shape makes them specific; link activity to temperature and pH.
Use the lock and key model to explain enzyme action.
Do rate calculations for chemical reactions.
Investigate how pH affects the rate at which amylase digests starch.
State where amylase, proteases and lipases are made and what each breaks down into what.
Explain that digestion makes small soluble molecules, used to build new molecules or for respiration.
Explain how bile neutralises stomach acid and emulsifies fat to speed lipase action.
Use Benedict's, iodine and Biuret reagents to test for sugars, starch, protein and lipids.
Describe the heart as a double circulation pump and name the main vessels attached to it.
Explain how the lungs are adapted for gas exchange: trachea, bronchi, alveoli, capillaries.
Describe how the natural pacemaker and artificial pacemakers control heart rate.
Explain how arteries, veins and capillaries are suited to their jobs, and calculate blood flow rate.
Describe blood as plasma with red cells, white cells and platelets, and state each function.
Recognise blood cell types in images and explain their adaptations.
Describe how fatty deposits narrow coronary arteries, and how stents and statins help.
Explain faulty valves, replacement valves, heart transplants and artificial hearts.
Evaluate drugs, mechanical devices and transplants as treatments for heart disease.
Define health and describe how communicable and non-communicable diseases and mental health interact.
Give examples of linked diseases: weak immunity, viruses and cancer, allergies, illness and depression.
Convert disease data between graphs and tables and use scatter diagrams to spot correlation.
Explain the principles of sampling for epidemiological data.
Discuss the human and financial cost of non-communicable diseases locally and globally.
Explain how diet, alcohol and smoking affect the incidence of non-communicable diseases.
Define risk factors and say which have proven causal mechanisms, such as smoking, alcohol, obesity and carcinogens.
Interpret charts, tables and scatter diagrams about risk factors.
Describe cancer as uncontrolled cell growth and division from changes in cells.
Distinguish benign tumours from malignant ones that spread and form secondary tumours.
State that cancer has lifestyle and genetic risk factors.
Explain how epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll, xylem, phloem, guard cells and meristems suit their functions.
Describe the roots, stem and leaves as a transport system and root hair cell adaptations.
Describe xylem carrying water and ions, strengthened by lignin, in the transpiration stream.
Describe phloem carrying dissolved sugars by translocation.
Describe the structure and role of stomata and guard cells in gas exchange and water loss.
Explain how temperature, humidity, air movement and light intensity change transpiration rate, and calculate that rate.
Plot and interpret graphs and data from stomata and transpiration investigations.
Explain that pathogens live in hosts and may damage them with toxins.
Name viruses, bacteria, protists and fungi as pathogens and how each spreads in animals and plants.
Describe how bacteria and viruses multiply and harm cells.
Explain how spread of disease can be reduced or prevented.
Describe measles: symptoms, droplet spread and vaccination.
Describe HIV, how it attacks immune cells, leads to AIDS and spreads.
Describe tobacco mosaic virus and its effect on plant growth.
Describe salmonella food poisoning: cause, spread, symptoms and control.
Describe gonorrhoea: symptoms, spread, antibiotic resistance and control.
Describe rose black spot, its effect on photosynthesis, spread and treatment.
Describe malaria as a protist disease spread by mosquitoes and how it is controlled.
Describe the non-specific defences: skin, nose, trachea and bronchi, stomach.
Explain how white blood cells defend by phagocytosis, antibodies and antitoxins.
Explain how vaccination gives immunity to an individual and protects a population.
Explain that antibiotics kill bacteria but not viruses, and that bacteria can become resistant.
Explain that painkillers treat symptoms and do not kill pathogens.
Describe how drugs were traditionally extracted from plants and microorganisms, with examples.
Describe preclinical and clinical trials testing toxicity, efficacy and dose, including double blind trials.
Give the photosynthesis word and symbol equation and describe it as endothermic using light energy.
Explain how temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll affect photosynthesis rate.
Measure rates and interpret graphs with one limiting factor.
Investigate how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed.
Explain graphs with two or three factors and identify the limiting factor.
Use the inverse square law for light intensity.
Explain how limiting factors affect greenhouse economics.
List the uses of glucose from photosynthesis, including storage and making cellulose and amino acids.
Explain that plants need nitrate ions to make proteins.
Describe respiration as exothermic and continuous, supplying energy for living processes.
Give the aerobic respiration equation and the muscle and yeast anaerobic equations.
Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration by oxygen need, products and energy released.
Describe fermentation in yeast and its use in bread and drinks.
Describe how heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume rise during exercise.
Explain lactic acid build-up, oxygen debt and muscle fatigue.
Explain how lactic acid is removed in the liver and what oxygen debt is.
Define metabolism and explain how sugars, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol are used to build and break down molecules.
Define homeostasis and name what is controlled: blood glucose, temperature, water.
Describe receptors, coordination centres and effectors in a control system.
Explain how the nervous system, neurones and CNS carry impulses from stimulus to response.
Explain how a reflex arc works and why reflexes matter.
Interpret nervous system data and investigate a factor affecting reaction time.
Describe hormones from glands travelling in blood to target organs, compared with nerves.
Describe the pituitary as a master gland and locate the main glands on a body diagram.
Explain how the pancreas and insulin lower blood glucose, with glycogen storage.
Compare Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes and their treatments.
Interpret graphs of blood glucose and insulin effects.
Explain how glucagon and insulin form a negative feedback cycle.
Describe the roles of oestrogen, testosterone and puberty hormones.
Describe the roles of FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone in the menstrual cycle.
Explain the interaction of the hormones in the menstrual cycle and interpret hormone graphs (higher).
Evaluate hormonal and non-hormonal methods of contraception.
Explain how FSH and LH fertility drugs work.
Describe the steps of IVF treatment.
Evaluate fertility treatment: stress, low success rates and multiple births.
Explain the roles of adrenaline in fight or flight and thyroxine in metabolic rate.
Explain thyroxine control by negative feedback.
Explain how variation, mutation and selection link inheritance to evolution and breeding.
Compare meiosis (non-identical cells) with mitosis (identical cells).
Describe sexual reproduction as gamete fusion giving variety, and asexual reproduction giving clones.
Explain how meiosis makes four different gametes with half the chromosomes, restored at fertilisation.
Describe DNA as a double helix polymer in chromosomes, and a gene as a section coding for a protein.
Define the genome and discuss why the human genome matters for medicine and migration studies.
Explain gamete, chromosome, gene, allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, genotype, phenotype.
Explain dominant and recessive alleles and why most traits involve many genes.
Complete Punnett squares and give outcomes as probabilities, ratios and from family trees.
Construct a genetic cross and predict outcomes using probability (higher).
Describe polydactyly (dominant) and cystic fibrosis (recessive) as inherited disorders.
Make informed judgements on the economic, social and ethical issues of embryo screening.
Explain the XX and XY sex chromosomes and use a genetic cross to show sex inheritance.
Describe how genes and environment shape the phenotype and cause variation.
Explain that variants arise from mutation, mostly with no effect, rarely changing phenotype.
Describe evolution as a change in inherited characteristics over time through natural selection.
Explain how selection of best-suited phenotypes drives evolution.
Explain how populations that cannot interbreed to give fertile offspring become new species.
Describe the process of selective breeding and give examples of chosen characteristics.
Explain benefits and risks of selective breeding, including inbreeding.
Describe genetic engineering as adding a gene from another organism, with crop and insulin examples.
Explain benefits, risks and objections around GM crops and medical gene modification.
Describe the steps: enzymes isolate a gene, a vector inserts it, early-stage cells develop with the trait.
Describe fossils and antibiotic-resistant bacteria as evidence for Darwin's theory.
Describe the three ways fossils form and why the fossil record is incomplete.
Interpret charts, graphs and evolutionary trees.
Define extinction and describe factors that contribute to it.
Explain how mutation and selection produce antibiotic-resistant strains like MRSA.
Describe how to slow resistance: sensible prescribing, finishing courses, restricting farm use.
Explain why new antibiotics are slow and costly to develop.
Describe Linnaeus's classification levels and binomial naming.
Describe how better microscopes and chemistry led to the three-domain system and use evolutionary trees.
Explain how the Sun and recycled materials sustain ecosystems.
Describe levels of organisation in an ecosystem and interdependence and competition.
Suggest what organisms compete for and how they are adapted in a given habitat.
Describe a stable community and interpret data on interactions within it.
List abiotic factors and explain how a change in one affects a community.
List biotic factors and explain how a change in one affects a community.
Explain structural, behavioural and functional adaptations, including extremophiles.
Describe producers and food chains, with consumers, predators and prey.
Interpret predator-prey cycle graphs.
Use quadrats and transects, calculate mean, mode and median, and measure a species' population size.
Explain the carbon cycle and water cycle and their importance to living things.
Explain the role of microorganisms in returning carbon dioxide and mineral ions.
Define biodiversity and explain why high biodiversity keeps ecosystems stable.
Describe water, air and land pollution from waste and its effect on biodiversity.
Explain how building, quarrying, farming, dumping and peat destruction reduce habitats and release carbon dioxide.
Explain why tropical deforestation occurs and evaluate its effects.
Describe rising carbon dioxide and methane and the biological consequences of global warming.
Describe positive and negative human impacts on biodiversity.
Describe programmes that protect biodiversity: breeding, habitat protection, hedgerows, lower emissions, recycling.
State the key ideas of biology: molecules, cells, ecosystems, photosynthesis, respiration, cycling, genomes, evolution.

topics.title: 5.1 Atomic structure and the periodic table

outcomes.text: Explain how the periodic table is organised and why it supports the nuclear model with electron energy levels.
Describe atoms as the smallest part of an element, shown by chemical symbols in the periodic table.
Describe compounds as elements chemically combined in fixed proportions, separable only by reactions.
Name and write symbols for the first 20 elements, Groups 1 and 7, and named compounds.
Write word equations, formulae and balanced symbol equations for reactions in the specification.
Write balanced half equations and ionic equations (higher).
Describe a mixture as unbonded substances whose chemical properties are unchanged.
Describe filtration, crystallisation, simple and fractional distillation and chromatography.
Choose a suitable separation method for a given mixture.
Describe the atom before and after the electron: indivisible sphere to plum pudding model.
Explain how alpha scattering led to the nuclear model replacing plum pudding.
Describe Bohr's orbits, the proton and Chadwick's neutron.
State the relative charges of protons, neutrons and electrons and why atoms are neutral.
Define atomic number and use the nuclear model to describe atoms.
State atom and nucleus sizes and that nearly all mass is in the nucleus.
Define mass number and isotopes, and work out protons, neutrons and electrons.
Define relative atomic mass and calculate it from isotope abundances.
Write electron arrangements for the first 20 elements as numbers and diagrams.
Explain that elements are in order of atomic number, with groups sharing outer electron numbers.
Explain how position relates to electron arrangement and predict reactivity.
Describe early tables by atomic weight and Mendeleev's gaps and predictions.
Define metals by positive ions, locate them in the table and explain differences from non-metals.
Explain how atomic structure and reactions relate to table position.
Describe noble gases as unreactive because of stable outer shells and explain boiling point trends.
Describe alkali metal reactions with oxygen, chlorine and water and the rising reactivity down the group.
Explain Group 1 properties from the single outer electron and predict trends.
Describe halogens as non-metal diatomic molecules and the compounds they form with metals and non-metals.
Explain trends down Group 7: melting point, boiling point, falling reactivity and displacement.

topics.title: 5.2 Bonding, structure, and the properties of matter

outcomes.text: Explain how bonding and structure determine material properties.
Describe ionic, covalent and metallic bonding and which substances have each.
Explain bonding in terms of electrostatic forces and electron transfer or sharing.
Describe electron transfer from metals to non-metals forming ions with noble gas structures.
Draw dot and cross diagrams for Group 1 and 2 metals with Group 6 and 7 non-metals.
Work out ion charges from group numbers.
Describe an ionic compound as a giant lattice held by electrostatic attraction, like sodium chloride.
Deduce ionic structures from diagrams, state limitations of models, and find empirical formulae.
Describe covalent bonds as shared pairs of electrons in small molecules, polymers and giant structures.
Draw dot and cross diagrams for common molecules like water, ammonia and methane.
Represent covalent structures, state model limitations and deduce molecular formulae.
Describe metals as giant structures of atoms with delocalised outer electrons.
Describe solids, liquids and gases with the particle model and state changes.
Explain why stronger forces between particles give higher melting and boiling points.
Predict states from data and explain the limitations of the simple particle model (higher).
Use (s), (l), (g) and (aq) in equations.
Explain high melting points and conduction when molten or dissolved for ionic compounds.
Explain low melting points and non-conduction using weak intermolecular forces.
Explain why larger molecules have higher melting and boiling points.
Explain why polymers are solid at room temperature and recognise them from diagrams.
Explain the very high melting points of giant covalent substances like diamond, graphite and silica.
Explain high melting points, bending and shaping of metals by their layers of atoms.
Explain why alloys are harder than pure metals.
Explain why metals conduct electricity and heat using delocalised electrons.
Explain diamond's hardness, melting point and non-conduction from its bonding.
Explain graphite's layers, slipperiness and conduction using delocalised electrons.
Describe graphene, fullerenes, Buckminsterfullerene and carbon nanotubes and their uses.
Use quantitative methods to find formulae, purity and yield.
State the law of conservation of mass and balance symbol equations, using multipliers and subscripts.
Calculate relative formula mass and percentage by mass of an element in a compound.
Show that reactant and product relative formula masses balance in an equation.
Explain apparent mass changes when a gas reacts or escapes in open systems.
Represent a spread of results and estimate uncertainty using the range around the mean.
Define the mole and Avogadro constant, linking one mole's mass to relative formula mass.
Convert between mass and moles using relative formula mass.
Interpret equations in moles and calculate reactant and product masses from a balanced equation.
Balance an equation from reacting masses by converting to moles and whole-number ratios.
Explain how a limiting reactant restricts the amount of product, in moles or grams.
Calculate the mass of solute in a given volume of solution in g/dm3.
Explain how solute mass and solution volume relate to concentration (higher).
Use chemical changes to predict new substances and extract resources.
Describe metals reacting with oxygen as oxidation, and define oxidation and reduction by oxygen.
Describe the reactions of potassium to copper with water and dilute acids and order them by reactivity.
Explain reactivity as tendency to form positive ions, and deduce an order from experiments.
Explain that a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its compound.
Explain why unreactive metals occur native and others need chemical extraction.
Describe extraction of metals less reactive than carbon by reduction with carbon.
Identify what is oxidised and reduced in extraction using oxygen gain and loss.
Define oxidation and reduction as loss and gain of electrons.
Write ionic equations for displacement and identify the species oxidised and reduced.
Describe acids reacting with magnesium, zinc and iron to make a salt and hydrogen.
Explain these as redox reactions and identify oxidised and reduced species (higher).
Describe neutralisation by alkalis, bases and carbonates producing salts, water and carbon dioxide.
Predict the salt from the acid used and the positive ion, and write salt formulae from ions.
Describe making a pure dry salt by adding excess insoluble solid to acid, filtering and crystallising.
Describe acids as producing H+ and alkalis OH-, and neutralisation as H+ plus OH- making water.
Use universal indicator or a pH probe and the 0 to 14 scale to identify acidic, neutral and alkaline solutions.
Distinguish strong from weak acids by ionisation and dilute from concentrated by amount.
Relate each pH unit to a factor of ten in hydrogen ion concentration.
Describe electrolytes and ions moving to the cathode and anode so elements form.
Write half equations for electrode reactions (higher).
Predict products of electrolysing a molten binary ionic compound, like lead bromide.
Explain when electrolysis is used for extraction and why it costs a lot of energy.
Describe aluminium extraction: why cryolite is added and why the carbon anode is replaced.
Predict products at each electrode for aqueous solutions from relative reactivity, water and halide ions.
Investigate the electrolysis of aqueous solutions with inert electrodes.
Describe cathode reduction and anode oxidation and write half equations.
Describe energy transfers by bond breaking and making in everyday reactions.
Explain energy conservation in reactions and why products have less energy if energy is released.
Describe exothermic reactions with uses such as hand warmers, and endothermic ones such as sports packs.
Classify reactions from temperature change and investigate variables affecting it.
Define activation energy as the minimum energy for particles to react.
Draw and read reaction profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions.
Explain that bond breaking takes in energy and bond making releases it.
Calculate overall energy change from bond energies and relate it to exothermic or endothermic.

topics.title: 5.6 The rate and extent of chemical change

outcomes.text: Optimise rate and yield in industrial reactions.
Calculate mean rate from reactant used or product formed over time, in g/s or cm3/s.
Draw and interpret quantity-time graphs and use tangents to find rate.
Use moles and mol/s, and calculate tangent gradients at a given time (higher).
List concentration, pressure, surface area, temperature and catalysts as factors that change reaction rate.
Investigate how concentration affects rate by gas volume or turbidity.
Explain that reactions need collisions with at least the activation energy.
Explain effects of concentration, pressure, temperature and surface area on rate using collision theory.
Describe catalysts as speeding reactions without being used up, by lowering activation energy.
Identify catalysts from their effect and absence from the equation, and draw a catalysed profile.
Describe reversible reactions, and that conditions can change their direction.
Explain that energy transfers are equal and opposite in forward and reverse directions.
Define equilibrium as equal forward and reverse rates in a closed system.
Use Le Chatelier's principle to predict how a system counteracts a change.
Predict the effect of changing concentration on equilibrium.
Predict the effect of temperature on equilibrium for exothermic and endothermic reactions.
Predict the effect of pressure on gaseous equilibrium from molecule counts.
Explain why carbon forms so many compounds, used as fuels and feedstock.
Describe crude oil as a finite resource from ancient plankton and a mixture mostly of hydrocarbons.
Give the alkane general formula CnH2n+2, name the first four and recognise alkanes.
Explain how fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions by evaporation and condensation.
Name fuels and petrochemical products made from fractions.
State how boiling point, viscosity and flammability change as molecules get bigger.
Write balanced equations for complete combustion of a hydrocarbon to carbon dioxide and water.
Describe catalytic and steam cracking conditions and why cracking is useful for small-molecule fuels.
Balance cracking equations and describe alkenes as reactive hydrocarbons used to make polymers.
Recall that bromine water goes colourless with an alkene.
Use chemical tests and instrumental methods to analyse substances.
Define a pure substance and use melting and boiling point data to tell pure from impure.
Describe formulations as designed mixtures with measured components and identify examples.
Explain how paper chromatography separates mixtures using mobile and stationary phases.
Interpret chromatograms, calculate Rf values and tell pure from impure substances.
Separate and compare coloured substances by paper chromatography.
Test for hydrogen with a burning splint and its pop.
Test for oxygen with a glowing splint that relights.
Test for carbon dioxide with limewater turning milky.
Test for chlorine with damp litmus paper that bleaches.
Explain how the atmosphere changes and how pollutants are tackled.
Give the approximate proportions of nitrogen, oxygen and other gases in the air.
Describe a theory of the early atmosphere from volcanic gases and the formation of oceans.
Evaluate theories of the early atmosphere given evidence.
Explain how algae and plants raised oxygen through photosynthesis.
Explain how carbon dioxide fell through photosynthesis, sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels.
Describe how limestone, coal, crude oil and natural gas formed.
Name water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane as greenhouse gases and explain the greenhouse effect with radiation.
Recall two human activities that increase carbon dioxide and two that increase methane.
Evaluate evidence quality on climate change, uncertainty and peer review.
Describe four potential effects of climate change and discuss their scale and risk.
Define carbon footprint and describe ways to cut carbon dioxide and methane, and why they are limited.
Describe how fuels produce carbon monoxide, soot, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.
Predict combustion products from a fuel's composition and conditions.
Describe and explain problems from carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulates.
Use resources sustainably and reduce waste and environmental impact.
Give natural products replaced by agricultural or synthetic ones and tell finite from renewable resources.
Define sustainable development and interpret resource data using orders of magnitude.
Distinguish potable water from pure water.
Describe producing potable water: fresh source, filter beds, sterilising.
Describe desalination by distillation or reverse osmosis and its energy cost.
Analyse and purify water samples for pH, dissolved solids and distillation.
Describe sewage treatment: screening, sedimentation, anaerobic digestion, aerobic treatment.
Compare the ease of getting potable water from waste, ground and salt water.
Describe phytomining and bioleaching for low-grade copper ores.
Evaluate biological extraction methods and recover copper by displacement or electrolysis.
Describe the stages of a life cycle assessment and why it is not wholly objective.
Carry out a simple comparative life cycle assessment of plastic and paper bags.
Explain how reuse and recycling of metals, glass and plastics cut resource, energy and waste use.
Evaluate ways of reducing the use of limited resources.
State the key ideas of chemistry: atoms, periodicity, bonding, structure, rates, reaction types, energy conservation.
Describe energy as stored, transferred and conserved, with efficiency and resources in mind.
Define a system and describe changes in energy stores for common situations like a kettle or a slowing vehicle.
Calculate energy changes from heating, work by forces and work by current.
Calculate kinetic energy from mass and speed.
Calculate elastic potential energy of a stretched spring.
Calculate gravitational potential energy from mass, gravitational field strength and height.
Define specific heat capacity and calculate thermal energy change from mass, c and temperature change.
Determine specific heat capacity of a material by experiment.
Define power as rate of energy transfer or work, and calculate it in watts.
Give examples showing power, such as two motors lifting the same load at different speeds.
State that energy is conserved, with no net change in a closed system, and describe dissipation.
Explain lubrication and thermal insulation and how wall thickness and conductivity affect a building's cooling.
Calculate efficiency from energy or power, as a decimal or percentage.
Describe ways to increase efficiency of an energy transfer (higher).
List the main energy resources and tell renewable from non-renewable.
Compare uses in transport, electricity and heating, and why some resources are more reliable.
Describe environmental impacts, trends in use, and limits on dealing with issues for political or economic reasons.
Use circuits and mains electricity safely and sustainably.
Draw and interpret circuit diagrams with standard symbols.
State that a closed circuit needs a source of potential difference for charge to flow.
Define current as rate of charge flow and use Q = I t.
Relate current to potential difference and resistance and use V = I R.
Investigate wire length and series and parallel resistors using circuit diagrams.
Distinguish ohmic conductors from lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs.
Describe a filament lamp's rising resistance and a diode's one-way current.
Describe thermistor and LDR resistance changes and uses like thermostats and light switches.
Design a circuit to measure resistance and read I-V graphs as linear or non-linear.
Compare current, potential difference and resistance in series and in parallel.
Calculate currents, potential differences and total resistance in series circuits.
Explain why more series resistors raise total resistance and more parallel ones lower it.
State mains is ac at 50 Hz and about 230 V, and explain ac versus dc.
Give the colours and roles of live, neutral and earth wires in a three-core cable.
Explain why a live wire is dangerous even with a switch open and why live-to-earth links are risky.
Calculate power using P = V I and P = I2 R.
Describe energy transfers in appliances and calculate E = P t and E = Q V.
Relate power ratings to energy changes in everyday appliances.
Describe the National Grid and the role of step-up and step-down transformers.
Explain why the National Grid is an efficient way to transfer energy.
Use the transformer equation for potential difference and current (higher).
Use the particle model to explain states, density, heating and gas pressure.
Calculate density from mass and volume and explain density differences between states.
Draw simple particle diagrams of solids, liquids and gases.
Measure the density of regular and irregular solids and liquids.
Describe state changes as physical, reversible and mass-conserving.
Define internal energy as total kinetic and potential energy of particles and how heating changes it.
Calculate temperature-change energy with specific heat capacity.
Define latent heat and calculate energy for a change of state with E = m L.
Interpret heating and cooling graphs and distinguish specific heat from latent heat.
Explain how gas molecule motion relates to temperature and pressure.
Explain how temperature affects pressure at constant volume.
Describe atoms, isotopes and radioactivity, its uses and hazards.
Describe the nuclear atom, its size and how electrons change level by absorbing or emitting radiation.
Define atomic number, mass number and isotopes, and the formation of positive ions.
Relate isotope differences to their notation.
Describe the plum pudding and nuclear models and why scattering evidence replaced the first.
Describe Bohr's electron orbits and the discovery of the proton and neutron.
Describe radioactive decay as random, with activity in becquerels and count rate.
Describe alpha, beta, gamma and neutron radiation and compare their penetration, range and ionising power.
Evaluate the best radiation source for a given use.
Write balanced nuclear equations for alpha and beta decay using atomic and mass numbers.
State how alpha, beta and gamma emission change the nucleus.
Define half-life and link it to the random nature of decay.
Find half-life from data and calculate the decline after several half-lives as a ratio (higher).
Distinguish contamination from irradiation and compare their hazards.
Explain why radiation studies need peer review and safe precautions.
Analyse forces in machines, structures and movement.
Distinguish scalar from vector quantities and represent vectors with arrows.
Define a force and give contact and non-contact force examples.
Describe force pairs between two objects as vectors.
Define weight and relate it to gravitational field strength.
Calculate weight using W = m g and describe centre of mass and the newtonmeter.
Explain a resultant force and calculate it for two forces in a straight line.
Draw free body diagrams, resolve forces into components and use scale vector diagrams.
Define work done and calculate it with W = F s.
Convert newton-metres to joules and link friction work to temperature rise.
Give examples of stretching, bending and compressing forces and explain why two forces are needed.
Distinguish elastic from inelastic deformation.
Use F = k e for stretching and compression, and describe linear and non-linear force-extension.
Calculate a spring constant and the elastic energy stored, and investigate force and extension.
Describe motion along a line and apply Newton's laws to forces, braking and momentum.
Distinguish distance (scalar) from displacement (vector) and give displacement with direction.
Recall typical speeds of walking, running, cycling, sound and wind.
Measure distance and time to calculate speed and use s = v t, including average speed.
Explain speed versus velocity, and circular motion's constant speed but changing velocity (higher).
Draw and interpret distance-time graphs and find speed from the gradient.
Use tangents to find speed of an accelerating object (higher).
Calculate acceleration from change in velocity over time and estimate everyday accelerations.
Use v squared minus u squared equals 2 a s for uniform acceleration.
Find acceleration from a velocity-time graph gradient and distance from the area (higher).
Describe free fall at about 9.8 m/s2 and terminal velocity when the resultant force is zero.
Apply the First Law: zero resultant force means constant velocity.
Define inertia as the tendency to keep the state of motion (higher).
State acceleration is proportional to resultant force and inversely proportional to mass.
Calculate with F = m a and estimate everyday road transport forces.
Define inertial mass as force over acceleration (higher).
Investigate how force and mass change acceleration.
Apply the Third Law of equal and opposite interaction forces to equilibrium.
Define stopping distance as thinking plus braking distance and relate it to speed.
Recall typical reaction times and factors like tiredness, alcohol and distraction.
Explain methods to measure reaction time and evaluate effects on thinking distance.
Explain how road, weather, brakes and tyres change braking distance and safety.
Estimate stopping distances over typical speeds.
Explain how braking friction reduces kinetic energy and heats the brakes.
Explain dangers of large decelerations and estimate braking forces (higher).
Define and calculate momentum with p = m v.
Apply conservation of momentum to collisions in closed systems.
Describe waves carrying energy and information.
Distinguish transverse from longitudinal waves with compression and rarefaction.
Describe evidence that waves transfer energy, not the medium itself.
Define amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period and use T = 1/f.
Use the wave equation v = f lambda and identify amplitude and wavelength from diagrams.
Describe methods to measure the speed of sound in air and ripples on water.
Choose apparatus to measure frequency, wavelength and speed in a ripple tank and a solid.
Describe electromagnetic waves as transverse, same speed in vacuum, and list the spectrum in order.
Give examples of energy transfer by electromagnetic waves.
Construct ray diagrams for refraction at a boundary.
Explain absorption, transmission, reflection and refraction varying with wavelength, using wave fronts and speed change.
Investigate how a surface affects infrared absorbed or radiated.
Explain that ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays harm tissue, depending on type and dose.
